extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of scientific method; experimental scientists; philosophers of science
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on using the principal methods of scientific induction (Agreement, Difference, Concomitant Variations, Residues) with examples from chemistry, electricity, meteorology, and physiology; includes cautions about extrapolation, controls, and corroboration by deduction and experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: When various instances that exhibit the same effect are compared, the antecedent circumstance common to all is inferred to be a cause (or part of the cause) of the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply by collecting diverse instances sharing the effect and identifying a common antecedent. Example: metallic poisons (arsenious acid, lead salts, etc.) all combine with animal tissues to form compounds resistant to putrefaction, indicating that such combination is the proximate cause of death. Use when many heterogeneous instances converge on a shared antecedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare a positive instance (effect present) with a negative instance (effect absent) that agree in all respects except one circumstance; the differing circumstance is inferred as the cause (or an essential condition) of the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires as nearly as possible identical conditions except for the single antecedent. Use examples like antidotes (e.g., hydrated peroxide of iron preventing arsenious acid poisoning) or controlled cases where the same substance is present but prevented from forming the active compound. Beware that if the positive and negative differ in many properties (even if nominally one substance), strict requirements are not met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect/Joint Method of Agreement and Difference (Indirect Method of Difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the strict conditions of the Method of Difference cannot be obtained, combine many agreeing instances and many negative instances and look for a circumstance present in all positives and absent in all negatives; convergence across many substances can approximate the rigor of Method of Difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when single perfectly controlled contrasts are unavailable. Example: multiple different antidotes all share the property of forming insoluble compounds with poisons; this multiplicity reduces the chance that some other shared property explains the result. Explicitly acknowledge residual uncertainty because many substances have many properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Concomitant Variations
rubrics_metrics.description: If changes in the magnitude or intensity of an antecedent are associated with systematic changes in the magnitude or intensity of a consequent, infer a causal relation or dependence between them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek proportional relationships (_cæteris paribus_) between antecedent and effect across a range of variation. Example: the capacity of neighboring bodies to support opposite electricity limits how much a conductor can be charged. Caution: narrow observational ranges can make very different laws appear numerically similar; avoid over-extrapolation from small variation ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Residues
rubrics_metrics.description: Subtract from a complex phenomenon the parts that can be explained by known causes; the remainder (residue) is attributed to the remaining, unknown cause(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use in combination with deduction and known laws; the text notes this method is not independent of deduction but still belongs among direct experimental methods. Provide explicit accounting of known contributions before inferring residual causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise definition and delimitation of the phenomenon under investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Before attempting induction, determine exactly what phenomenon is meant and exclude similar but distinct phenomena (e.g., separate dew from rain, fog moisture, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform preliminary operations to define terms and scope so that comparisons are meaningful. Example: define dew as 'spontaneous appearance of moisture on substances exposed in the open air when no rain or visible wet is falling.' This avoids conflating distinct phenomena that would invalidate inductive comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of contrary/negative cases (necessary for Method of Difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actively seek instances where the effect does not occur and compare them with instances where it does, to identify differing antecedents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative cases are essential to discriminate causes. Example: polished metals often do not dew while glass does; comparing such cases leads to investigation of substance, surface, and texture. Ensure negative cases are as similar as possible to positives except for the suspected causal factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroboration by Deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirm an inductive hypothesis by deducing consequences from established laws and checking whether those consequences are observed; deduction can strengthen causal claims and reveal additional necessary conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use known theoretical laws (e.g., laws of vapor pressure and heat) to deduce that cooling the surface will condense vapor, thereby corroborating the induction about dew. Deduction can also reveal auxiliary conditions (e.g., sufficient atmospheric moisture) that induction alone might miss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct experimental verification (manipulation of antecedent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Test causal hypotheses by experimentally altering the antecedent and observing whether the consequent follows (Method of Difference in experimental form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform controlled experiments, e.g., artificially cool a surface to find the temperature at which dew forms. Even small-scale laboratory tests that reproduce the causal link increase confidence in generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of natural experiments (when nature introduces a single clear change)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and use naturally occurring events that introduce a clear change in antecedent conditions to test causal hypotheses when controlled experiments are impracticable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: withdrawal of clouds (clear openings) is a natural experiment that causes surface cooling and subsequent dew deposition; observing the effect during such natural changes can satisfy the requisitions of the Method of Difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of extrapolation beyond observed limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not assume that a law of variation observed within a limited range will hold outside that range without further evidence, because new agents or dormant properties may appear or different numerical laws may diverge at larger scales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly recognize uncertainty when extending conclusions beyond observed quantities. Example: empirical formulae for steam elasticity or fluid resistance failed when relied upon beyond the observation limits. Favor additional data over unsupported extrapolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about numerical indistinguishability within narrow ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: Different mathematical laws may produce very similar numerical results within a narrow observation window, making it easy to mistake the true law when variations observed are small relative to total quantities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inferring a precise numerical law from data covering only a narrow range; seek observations across wider ranges or other methods of corroboration to distinguish competing functional forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensiveness in surveying analogous instances
rubrics_metrics.description: When forming a general law, examine all known modes or varieties of the phenomenon to see whether the proposed concomitant or antecedent is invariable across them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in induced electricity, survey electrical machine, Leyden jar, magnetism, voltaic circuits, etc., to see if opposite electricity is always excited. A broad survey strengthens claims from the Method of Agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for multiple contributing factors and resolving confounders
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that several distinct qualities (e.g., substance, surface, texture) may each influence the phenomenon; disentangle them by varying one factor at a time and using appropriate methods (agreement, difference, concomitant variations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: dew depends on conductivity, radiative properties, and texture; show how texture relates to conductivity/radiation and use repeated applications of concomitant variation to isolate primary causes. Use hierarchical or corroborative inductions to sort primary from secondary causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of antidotes/control agents as decisive tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce substances known to neutralize or prevent the hypothesized causal antecedent (antidotes) to show that when the antecedent is neutralized the effect disappears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: hydrated peroxide of iron prevents arsenious acid poisoning by forming an insoluble compound; sugar neutralizes copper salts; sulphuric acid lemonade prevents lead poisoning. Such agents provide strong instances for Method of Difference if their neutralizing mechanism is known and singular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangulation of methods for high assurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine multiple methods of induction (Agreement, Difference, Concomitant Variations), direct experiment, natural experiments, and deduction to reach the highest attainable certainty about causal laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes that practices combining several methods yield fuller assurance than any single method alone — e.g., the theory of dew is supported by agreement, difference, concomitant variations, deduction, direct experiment, and natural observation of cloud cover changes.
